analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers again sell short-term health plans of up to 12 months, exempt from Affordable Care Act protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out a 2016 federal rule that limited "short-term, limited-duration" health plans to less than three months, restoring the older definition that allowed such plans to run up to 12 months. Short-term plans don't have to follow Affordable Care Act rules — they can deny people with preexisting conditions and skip required benefits — so they can be much cheaper for healthy buyers, but siphoning healthy people out of the regular market raises premiums for everyone else. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to three committees, sent to a health subcommittee, and expired at the end of the Congress without a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Healthy people who want a cheaper, less comprehensive insurance option, and the insurers that sell short-term plans, which could again offer year-long policies without meeting Affordable Care Act requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Healthy buyers and short-term plan insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the Health, Treasury, and Labor departments to discard the 2016 rule's new definition of short-term insurance and go back to the prior definition, under which a short-term plan could last up to 12 months instead of less than three.

Because short-term plans are exempt from Affordable Care Act market rules (such as covering preexisting conditions), they can be priced far below ACA-compliant plans, giving healthy people a cheaper option.

The bill was largely redundant in practice: a separate 2018 rule, already in effect since October 2018, had already raised the maximum duration of short-term plans to under 12 months initially and up to 36 months with renewals, so the bill would mainly have reinforced a change that had already happened.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions and anyone who needs comprehensive coverage. As healthier people buy short-term plans instead, the ACA-compliant risk pool gets sicker and more expensive, so premiums rise for those who remain; anyone buying a short-term plan can also be left with uncovered bills because these plans skip required benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and ACA enrollees

drawbacks.text: Short-term plans are exempt from Affordable Care Act requirements, including coverage of people with preexisting conditions, so a person who buys one can be denied coverage for an existing illness or left with large uncovered medical bills.
Pulling healthy people out of ACA-compliant plans makes the remaining risk pool sicker, which pushes premiums up for everyone who stays — the standard adverse-selection cost of exempt plans.

The bill's core change was already accomplished by the 2018 rule, which allows short-term plans of up to 12 months initially and up to 36 months with renewals, so enacting it would have added little for consumers while making the longer-duration plans harder for a future administration to reverse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: healthy buyers would get a cheaper, skimpier option for up to a year. The cost lands on a different group of ordinary people — those with preexisting conditions, who face higher premiums in the regulated market and no protection under these plans. Because the 2018 rule had already allowed year-long plans, the bill's main practical effect would have been to lock that loosening in by statute, making it harder to undo. On balance, the bill traded broad consumer protections for a cheaper product available only to the healthiest customers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Fortenberry introduced the bill on January 10, 2019, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor Committees, and later to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No committee took it up further, and it received no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The 2018 rule allowing short-term plans of up to 12 months initially, and up to 36 months with renewals, remained in effect regardless, so the bill's failure changed little in practice.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one's position changed much. Insurers selling short-term plans kept offering them under the 2018 rule without needing this bill, while the higher premiums that exempt plans create for ACA enrollees also continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Short-term plan sellers; little else changed

against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill and no one — Republican or Democrat — cosponsored it; no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split shows up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have re-legalized year-long plans that skip Affordable Care Act rules, letting these insurers price cheap policies for healthy customers. Their gain comes from enrolling healthy people whose premiums then don't help cover the sick, which drives up costs in the regulated market.

Losing healthy enrollees to exempt short-term plans raises average claims in ACA-compliant risk pools, forcing higher premiums for plans that must cover everyone. In this specific fight their interest ran alongside the people most at risk of losing coverage.
